title: Solomon's request (1 Kings 3:5–14)
hookLine: asked what he wants, a young king asks for an understanding heart

lines: ASK WHAT I SHALL GIVE THEE.
cards: "Ask what I shall give thee." No conditions, no small print. The new king Solomon has gone to Gibeon to offer sacrifices, and that night, in a dream, God appears to him and says it.
Ask. It's the old game of one wish, except here God is asking, and the one being asked is young, newly crowned, with his father David gone and a whole kingdom watching. What would anyone ask for?
Money that never runs out. A long life. Enemies out of the way.
Solomon asks for none of them.

teach.h: I AM BUT A LITTLE CHILD.
teach.b: He starts by being honest about himself, in the King James Bible: "I am but a little child: I know not how to go out or come in." A king, admitting he doesn't know how to do the job.
Then the request: "Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad."

In Hebrew, an understanding heart is lev shomea: literally, a hearing heart, a listening heart. Some readers point out that in the Bible's way of speaking, the heart is where you think and decide, not only feel.

teach.h: NOT FOR HIMSELF, FOR HIS PEOPLE.
teach.b: So Solomon asks for a mind that listens: to people, to both sides of a case, to God. And it isn't for himself. To judge thy people.
The speech pleased the Lord, and God names what Solomon didn't ask for: "thou hast not asked for thyself long life; neither hast asked riches for thyself, nor hast asked the life of thine enemies."
Then the turn: God gives the wise and understanding heart, and adds what he didn't ask for, riches and honor, and long life if he walks in God's ways.

Some Christians connect this with a line from the Gospels: seek first the kingdom of God, and the rest will be added. The letter of James puts it plainly: "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God."
The story doesn't promise Solomon always used his gift well; later chapters are honest about that. But on this night, with anything on offer, he asked for a listening heart.

how: Some Christians pray for wisdom with Solomon's request in mind, and some point to James 1:5, which invites anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God for it.

asking to build the temple in his own name
asking for a listening heart, not riches

games.q: you're young and newly crowned. in a dream God says: ask what I shall give thee. what do you ask for?
o: riches enough for the whole kingdom.
a long life to rule well.
an understanding heart to judge your people.
games.why: "Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart." the speech pleased the Lord, and the rest was added.

practice: Choose one situation where you don't know what to do, and notice what you'd normally wish for: that it would go away, or go your way. Set that wish down and ask instead for a listening heart for this one thing.
If you pray, ask God in your own words, or borrow Solomon's: an understanding heart; if you don't, simply hold the situation and listen.

wordCard.voice: Solomon's request. Offered anything at all, the young king asked for an understanding heart, to judge his people well.

orig.note: Hebrew: a hearing heart, the phrase the King James renders an understanding heart (1 Kings 3:9).

carryVoice: Your line: an understanding heart. Given any wish, he chose a heart that listens. Rest well.
